title: What Lightning Actually Does To Your Body
sources: Roy Sullivan, a US park ranger at Shenandoah National Park, was struck by lightning seven times between 1942 and 1977 and survived all of them (Guinness World Records)
Lightning can heat the air around it to about 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, roughly five times hotter than the surface of the sun (US National Weather Service)
Much of a lightning current can flow over the outside of the body (the flashover effect), which is one reason most victims survive (NWS; Cooper, 'Lightning injuries', Medscape)
About 90 percent of people struck by lightning survive (US National Weather Service, CDC)
Cardiac arrest is the main cause of death from lightning: the current can stop the heart (Cooper 1980, Annals of Emergency Medicine; CDC)
Lichtenberg figures: fern-like red marks on the skin of some lightning survivors, appearing within an hour and usually fading within a day or two (Cherington et al. 2007, NEJM images)
